title: Constructive 2D Borsuk-Ulam via Tucker's Lemma
description: The 2D Borsuk-Ulam theorem can be proved combinatorially via Tucker's 2D lemma, avoiding algebraic topology. Tucker's 2D lemma is stated as a single axiom (tucker_2d_grid) — the combinatorial path-following result for the triangulated grid — from which the logical chain Tucker 2D → approximate BU → exact BU is fully formalized. BU for linear maps is proved algebraically via rank-nullity.

meta.author: Formalized in Lean 4 (Mathlib)

axiomDetails: tucker_2d_grid: Tucker's 2D combinatorial lemma for the triangulated grid — an antipodally-labeled boundary forces an interior complementary edge (path-following in the simplicial complex). The earlier overly-general `tuckers_lemma` axiom was removed as unsound; `tucker_disk_approx_zero` is now proved from this axiom (tucker_disk_approx_zero_proved).
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: tucker_2d_grid. See Lean source for the complete statement.

overview.historicalContext: Tucker's lemma (1946) is the combinatorial analog of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem. While BU states that every continuous map from S^n to R^n has an antipodal pair, Tucker's lemma states that every antipodally-labeled triangulation of the disk has a complementary edge. The connection: discretize a continuous map via Tucker labeling, apply Tucker's lemma to find complementary edges, take limits to get exact antipodal pairs. This provides a constructive/combinatorial proof of BU, avoiding algebraic topology (degree theory, homology).
overview.problemStatement: Can the 2D Borsuk-Ulam theorem be proved constructively using Tucker's lemma instead of algebraic topology? We formalize the key combinatorial ingredient (Tucker 2D) and the logical reduction to BU.
overview.text: The 2D Borsuk-Ulam theorem can be proved combinatorially via Tucker's 2D lemma, avoiding algebraic topology. Tucker's 2D lemma is stated as a single axiom (tucker_2d_grid) — the combinatorial path-following result for the triangulated grid — from which the logical chain Tucker 2D → approximate BU → exact BU is fully formalized. BU for linear maps is proved algebraically via rank-nullity.
overview.proofStrategy: 1. Define Tucker labels {-2,-1,+1,+2} with negation and complementarity. 2. Prove the 1D Tucker lemma (tucker_1d). 3. State the general Tucker 2D lemma as a single axiom (tucker_2d_grid). 4. Build the logical chain: Tucker 2D -> approximate BU -> exact BU (tucker_disk_approx_zero_proved -> approx_borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected -> borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected). 5. Prove BU for linear maps algebraically as an alternative.
keyInsights: Tucker 2D is purely combinatorial and computationally verifiable for finite triangulations
The boundary parity theorem (even number of complementary boundary edges) is the key structural constraint that forces interior complements
The antipodal condition is NECESSARY: without it, constant labelings have no complementary edges
The only non-constructive step in Tucker -> BU is the compactness/limiting argument
For linear maps, BU reduces to rank-nullity (dim kernel >= 1)

sections.title: Part XXII — Grid Infrastructure

sections.title: Part XVII — Hemisphere Projection Infrastructure

sections.title: Part XXI — Uniform Continuity on the Compact Disk

sections.title: Part XXII — Radial Extension and Grid Elimination

sections.title: Part XXIII — Grid Labeling and Tucker Application
sections.summary: Finite-grid labeling for the Tucker application (9 declarations): `gridVertexFin`, `gridBoundaryFin`, `gridEdgesFin`/`gridEdgesTriFin`, and the antipodal involution `gridAntipodalFin` with its boundary-preservation lemmas.

sections.title: Part XXIII.5 — Path-Following Infrastructure for Tucker 2D
sections.summary: The largest block (19 declarations): the door-counting / path-following machinery for 2D Tucker — `GridTriangle`, `IsDoor`, `doorCount`, `DoorPath`, the parity arguments, and the file's sole `axiom tucker_2d_grid` (the 2D Tucker's lemma on the grid).

sections.title: Part XXIV — 2D Borsuk–Ulam from Tucker (Approximate and Exact)
sections.summary: The headline results: `approx_borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected` and `borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected`, followed by `#check` lines for the public API.

conclusion.summary: The formalization demonstrates that the 2D Borsuk-Ulam theorem has a purely combinatorial proof via Tucker's lemma. Tucker's 2D lemma is stated as a single axiom (tucker_2d_grid); the boundary-parity structure that motivates it is recorded as exposition (the `*_informal` lemmas state the parity intuition, with the deep combinatorial content carried in their docstrings rather than fully proved). The necessity of the antipodal condition is proved by counterexample. The logical chain Tucker → approximate BU → exact BU is formalized with 1 axiom and 0 sorries, and the exact result borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected follows by compactness. IVT on line segments extracts zeros from complementary edges.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: 1. BU is 'morally constructive': Tucker's lemma IS constructive; only the limiting argument requires classical analysis. 2. The boundary parity theorem is the structural invariant of Tucker labelings that motivates the single combinatorial axiom.

3. The framework is extensible: proving Tucker 2D generally (path-following in the simplicial complex) would eliminate the remaining combinatorial axiom.
openQuestions: Can Tucker's 2D lemma be proved formally in Lean using path-following in simplicial complexes, eliminating the tucker_2d_grid axiom?
Can the discretization step (Tucker labeling of continuous maps) be formalized without axioms?
Can small finite triangulations (e.g. 5-vertex disk, 9-vertex grid) be machine-checked by decide/native_decide to substantiate the axiom on finite cases?
Can the boundary parity theorem be proved structurally, replacing the current `*_informal` exposition with a full Lean proof?

Borsuk-Ulam implies Brouwer's fixed point theorem: if f: Bⁿ→Bⁿ had no fixed point, the retraction Bⁿ→Sⁿ⁻¹ would contradict BU. The constructive BU approach here suggests a constructive path to Brouwer via Tucker's lemma

mainTheorems.name: borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected
mainTheorems.statement: ∀ continuous f : S² → ℝ², ∃ x ∈ S², f x = f (−x)
mainTheorems.significance: The headline result: the exact 2-dimensional Borsuk–Ulam theorem, obtained constructively through Tucker's combinatorial lemma rather than the usual algebraic-topology machinery (degree theory / cohomology). Answers the open question in the affirmative.
mainTheorems.description: Minimizes d(x) = dist(f x, f(−x)) over the compact sphere S²; the approximate version forces the minimum to 0, and antipodal continuity upgrades the infimum to an attained exact coincidence.

mainTheorems.name: approx_borsuk_ulam_2d_corrected
mainTheorems.statement: ∀ continuous f : S² → ℝ², ∀ ε>0, ∃ x ∈ S², dist (f x) (f (−x)) < ε
mainTheorems.significance: The quantitative heart of the proof: for every tolerance ε there is a nearly-antipodal-coincident point. This is what Tucker's lemma delivers directly; the exact theorem is its compactness limit.
mainTheorems.description: Transfers tucker_disk_approx_zero_proved from the disk to the sphere via the diskToSphere parametrization, using that g = antisymmetricDiff3 f is odd and continuous on S².

mainTheorems.name: tucker_disk_approx_zero_proved
mainTheorems.statement: g continuous with odd boundary on D² ⟹ ∀ δ>0, ∃ w ∈ D², dist (g w) 0 < δ
mainTheorems.significance: The Part-XXIII capstone assembling the whole pipeline on the disk: an odd-on-the-boundary continuous field must come arbitrarily close to zero somewhere. This is where the Tucker axiom is actually consumed.
mainTheorems.description: Chains tucker_2d_grid (complementary edge exists) → complementary_edge_approx_dominant (edge ⟹ g small) → mesh_refinement_principle (refine the grid) → radial extension, letting the grid mesh → 0.

mainTheorems.name: tucker_2d_grid
mainTheorems.statement: For a signed labeling L of the (2N+1)×(2N+1) grid that is antipodal on the boundary, ∃ a complementary edge (u,v) ∈ gridEdgesTriFin N
mainTheorems.significance: The single assumption of the development: Tucker's lemma specialized to the triangulated square grid. Everything else in the file is proved from Mathlib; this combinatorial fixed-point statement is the one axiom (status: axiomatized, axiomCount 1).
mainTheorems.description: Stated after the triangulated-grid infrastructure (gridEdgesTriFin, gridBoundaryFin, gridAntipodalFin). The intended proof is the standard door-counting / parity argument on triangle boundaries, sketched informally in Part XXIII.

mainTheorems.name: tucker_1d
mainTheorems.statement: L : Fin(2N+1) → Bool with L 0 ≠ L (last) ⟹ ∃ i, L i.castSucc ≠ L i.succ
mainTheorems.significance: The one-dimensional Tucker lemma: an antipodally-labeled line must contain a sign-changing (complementary) edge. It is the base case and conceptual template for the 2D grid axiom.
mainTheorems.description: An immediate corollary of discrete_ivt applied to the boolean labeling on a path of 2N+1 vertices.

mainTheorems.name: discrete_ivt
mainTheorems.statement: f : Fin(n+1) → Bool with f 0 ≠ f (last) ⟹ ∃ i, f i.castSucc ≠ f i.succ
mainTheorems.significance: A discrete intermediate value theorem: a boolean sequence with differing endpoints must flip somewhere. This combinatorial IVT is the discrete analogue that replaces continuity arguments in the Tucker approach.
mainTheorems.description: By contradiction: if no adjacent pair differs, induction propagates f 0 to f (last), contradicting the endpoint hypothesis.

mainTheorems.name: dominantComponentLabel_antipodal
mainTheorems.significance: The labeling scheme is antipodal: negating a vector keeps the dominant coordinate but flips its sign bit. This is exactly the boundary-antipodal condition Tucker's lemma requires, linking the geometric odd field to the combinatorial labeling.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds dominantComponentLabel (dominant coordinate = larger |component|, sign = its sign) and uses abs_neg to see the magnitude comparison is invariant while the sign flips.

mainTheorems.name: complementary_edge_approx_dominant
mainTheorems.statement: g continuous, edge (u,v) with opposite dominant signs in coordinate k ⟹ g is small near the edge
mainTheorems.significance: Bridges combinatorics back to analysis: a Tucker complementary edge (labels +k and −k) forces the k-th component of g to change sign, so by the intermediate value theorem g is nearly zero along the edge.
mainTheorems.description: Applies the intermediate value theorem on the segment between u and v to the sign-changing coordinate (ivt_segment_fst/snd), then bounds the non-dominant coordinate via continuity.

mainTheorems.name: mesh_refinement_principle
mainTheorems.statement: g continuous on D², ε>0 ⟹ ∃ δ>0, close disk points have g-values within ε
mainTheorems.significance: Uniform continuity on the compact disk: refining the triangulation mesh below δ makes the approximate zeros genuinely small. This is what lets the sequence of ε-approximate coincidences converge to an exact one.
mainTheorems.description: Uniform continuity of g on the compact closed disk (closedDisk_isCompact + continuous ⟹ uniformly continuous) extracts the modulus δ for the given ε.

mainTheorems.name: radialExtend_zero_gives_disk_zero
mainTheorems.statement: dist (radialExtend g x) 0 < δ ⟹ ∃ w ∈ D², dist (g w) 0 < δ
mainTheorems.significance: Justifies the radial extension from the disk D² to the square [−1,1]²: a near-zero of the extended field yields a near-zero of the original field on the disk, so working on the square grid loses nothing.
mainTheorems.description: Case split on whether x lies inside the disk; outside, radialExtend projects x radially onto the boundary circle, and the boundary value coincides with a genuine disk value.

mainTheorems.name: mesh_refinement_square
mainTheorems.statement: h continuous on [−1,1]², ε>0 ⟹ ∃ δ>0, close square points have h-values within ε
mainTheorems.significance: The square-grid analogue of the disk mesh-refinement principle, needed because the Tucker grid lives on [−1,1]² rather than the disk. Ensures grid refinement controls the field on the square domain.
mainTheorems.description: Uniform continuity of h on the compact closed square [−1,1]² (closedSquare_isCompact) supplies the modulus δ.

mainTheorems.name: gridAntipodalFin_involution
mainTheorems.significance: The discrete antipodal map on the (2N+1)² grid is an involution — the combinatorial counterpart of x ↦ −x squaring to the identity. A structural prerequisite for a well-posed antipodal labeling.
mainTheorems.description: Both coordinates use Fin.rev; the identity is Fin.rev_rev (double reversal is the identity).

mainTheorems.name: gridAntipodalFin_maps_boundary
mainTheorems.statement: v ∈ gridBoundaryFin N ⟹ gridAntipodalFin N v ∈ gridBoundaryFin N
mainTheorems.significance: The grid antipodal map preserves the boundary, so the boundary-antipodal hypothesis of Tucker's lemma is meaningful and self-consistent on the triangulated grid.
mainTheorems.description: A boundary vertex has a coordinate equal to 0 or 2N; reversing (val ↦ 2N − val) sends 0 ↔ 2N, keeping the vertex on the boundary.

mainTheorems.name: antisymmetricDiff3_odd
mainTheorems.significance: The reduction that starts the whole proof: g(x) = f(x) − f(−x) is an odd field on S³ ⊂ ℝ³, converting the coincidence problem f(x)=f(−x) into finding a zero of an odd map — precisely Tucker's setting.
mainTheorems.description: Direct computation unfolding antisymmetricDiff3 and neg3 with neg3_neg3, then ext/ring on each component.

mainTheorems.name: antisymmetricDiff_eq_zero_iff
mainTheorems.statement: antisymmetricDiff f x = (0,0) ↔ f x = f (−x)
mainTheorems.significance: Pins the equivalence exploited throughout: a zero of the odd difference field is exactly an antipodal coincidence point of f. Reduces Borsuk–Ulam to a zero-finding problem.
mainTheorems.description: Unfolds antisymmetricDiff and rearranges the componentwise equalities f x − f(−x) = 0 into f x = f(−x).

mainTheorems.name: diskToSphere_on_sphere
mainTheorems.statement: p ∈ D² ⟹ diskToSphere p lands on S² (sum of squared coords = 1)
mainTheorems.significance: The explicit disk→hemisphere parametrization used to pull the sphere problem down to the planar disk where the grid/Tucker machinery lives, sending the disk onto the unit sphere.
mainTheorems.description: Computes the third coordinate as √(1 − p.1² − p.2²) and verifies p.1² + p.2² + (√…)² = 1 via Real.sq_sqrt on the nonnegative radicand.
